# gpcn_vpc_vpn_gateway (Resource)

A VPN gateway gives a VPC in GPCN™ (Global Private Cloud Network™) a public address for your VPN devices to connect to. Create it first, then add VPN connections. In some data centers it also takes a public address of its own and reserves a /28 from the VPC's range.

Manages the VPN gateway of a GPCN™ VPC. A VPC has at most one VPN gateway. It holds the VPN gateway address, the public IPv4 address your peer gateway connects to for site-to-site VPN. Your organization needs the Site-to-Site VPN feature, and the data center of the VPC must offer site-to-site VPN. The API key needs vpc:read to read the VPN gateway, and vpc-vpn-connection:create and vpc-vpn-connection:delete to manage it. A VPN gateway has no attribute that changes in place. A gateway that fails to build is replaced on the next apply.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# Example: A VPN gateway for a GPCN™ VPC
#
# A VPN gateway holds the VPN gateway address, the public address your peer
# gateway connects to for site-to-site VPN. A VPC has one. Your organization
# needs the Site-to-Site VPN feature, and the data center must offer
# site-to-site VPN.

terraform {
  required_providers {
    gpcn = {
      source  = "Global-Private-Cloud-Network/gpcn"
      version = "~>1.5.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "gpcn" {
  host = "https://api.gpcn.com"
}

# Lookup data center in Central US region
data "gpcn_datacenters" "central_us" {
  country_name = "United States"
  region_name  = "Central"
  name         = "Chicago 1"
}

resource "gpcn_vpc" "example" {
  name          = "terraform-demo-vpc"
  datacenter_id = data.gpcn_datacenters.central_us.datacenters[0].id
  cidr          = "10.60.0.0/16"
}

resource "gpcn_vpc_subnet" "example" {
  vpc_id = gpcn_vpc.example.id
  name   = "terraform-demo-web"
  cidr   = "10.60.1.0/24"
}

# The gateway waits for the subnet, because an appliance gateway reserves a
# /28 block inside the VPC CIDR.
resource "gpcn_vpc_vpn_gateway" "example" {
  vpc_id     = gpcn_vpc.example.id
  depends_on = [gpcn_vpc_subnet.example]
}

# Give this address to the administrator of your peer gateway
output "gpcn_vpc_vpn_gateway_address" {
  value = gpcn_vpc_vpn_gateway.example.address
}
```

## Before you start

A VPN gateway needs three things in place:

- Your organization has the Site-to-Site VPN feature turned on. Without it, GPCN™ refuses the create with a message that says so.
- The VPC's data center offers site-to-site VPN. The `vpn_capable` attribute of `gpcn_vpc` and of the `gpcn_datacenters` data source tells you before you apply.
- Your API key can read VPCs (`vpc:read`) and has the `vpc-vpn-connection:create` and `vpc-vpn-connection:delete` permissions.

## Gateway kinds

The data center decides how it provides the VPN gateway, and you can't choose. The `kind` attribute tells you which one you got.

- **`router`**: the data center's router carries the VPN. `reserved_block` is null, and nothing comes out of your VPC's range.
- **`appliance`**: the VPN gateway is its own appliance. It takes a public address of its own, and it reserves a /28 from the VPC's range, which `reserved_block` reports. The VPC needs a free /28, or the create fails.

For both kinds, `address` is the VPN gateway address, the public address your peer gateway connects to. Give it to whoever runs the device at your site. The example waits for the subnet before it creates the VPN gateway, because an appliance picks a free /28 and a subnet you create later can't overlap it.

## Failed gateways

If the VPN gateway fails to build, the apply reports the reason and Terraform marks the resource tainted. If a gateway reads as `failed` later, the next plan replaces it. GPCN™ can't retry a failed gateway, so Terraform deletes it and creates it again in one apply.

If a create times out, you interrupt it, or GPCN™ gives an unclear answer, Terraform marks the gateway tainted, and the next apply replaces it. Replacing an appliance gateway gives it a new VPN gateway address, so your peer gateway needs the new one. To keep the gateway instead, wait until it reads `ready`, then run `terraform untaint <address>`.

## Deleting

GPCN™ refuses to remove a VPN gateway while any VPN connection still uses it. When your connections set `vpn_gateway_id` to this resource's `id`, Terraform deletes them first. If you made the connections outside Terraform, delete them before you destroy the gateway.

Destroying a VPC also removes a VPN gateway that's left over, but GPCN™ refuses to delete a VPC while it still has any VPN connection.

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
## Schema

### Required

- `vpc_id` (String) Unique identifier of the VPC the VPN gateway belongs to. A VPC has one VPN gateway. Changing this value requires replacing the VPN gateway

### Read-Only

- `address` (String) Public IPv4 address of the VPN gateway. Give it to the administrator of your peer gateway, which connects to it
- `failure_reason` (String) Why the VPN gateway failed to build or to be removed, or null when neither happened
- `id` (String) Unique identifier for the VPN gateway in UUID format
- `kind` (String) How the data center provides the VPN gateway: 'router' or 'appliance'. The data center decides, and you can't choose
- `reserved_block` (String) The /28 block GPCN™ reserves inside the VPC CIDR for an appliance VPN gateway. It's null when the kind is 'router'
- `state` (String) Lifecycle state of the VPN gateway: one of 'creating', 'ready', 'failed' or 'removing'

## Import

Import is supported using the following syntax:

The [`terraform import` command](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/import) can be used, for example:

```shell
# A VPC has one VPN gateway, so the import ID is the ID of the VPC.
terraform import gpcn_vpc_vpn_gateway.example "c13808d9-3b7d-42c5-a21d-f0961308a38a"
```

A VPC has one VPN gateway, so the import ID is the ID of the VPC.
